title: Go live from a phone today
summary: Your first stream happens in this lesson, from the phone in your hand, in a Berbice room with Berbice light.
body: Every platform you already use can go live: TikTok (1,000 followers needed, or use a friend's account to practise), Instagram, Facebook, YouTube (50 subscribers needed for mobile live). Pick the one where your people already are.

Light: face the window, never sit with it behind you. Afternoon sun through a Berbice window is the best free light in the world. At night, one lamp in front of you and slightly above, never the ceiling bulb alone.

Framing: phone upright for TikTok and Instagram, sideways for YouTube and Facebook. Eyes one third from the top of the screen. Camera at eye level, so stack books under the phone if you have no tripod.
Sound: the phone mic is fine if the room is quiet and you are within one metre. Fans off. Dogs out. A towel on the table kills echo.
The first ten seconds: say who you are, where you are, and what is about to happen. People decide to stay in ten seconds.
steps: Charge the phone to 100% and turn on Do Not Disturb.
Open the platform, tap Live, write a title that says what you will do.
Check the picture, check the light, say the ten-second opener.
Stream for two minutes. Read every comment out loud.
Say goodbye, say when you are back, end the live.
assignment: A two-minute live on any platform. Screenshot the ended-live screen (viewers, time) and post it in the cohort group.

title: Your channel, your name
summary: Pick a handle you will not regret, set up two channels properly, and lock them so nobody takes them from you.
body: A handle is a name people type. Short, spellable when heard on radio, the same on every platform. Check it is free on Twitch, YouTube, TikTok and Instagram before you commit. Avoid numbers you will have to explain.
Profile picture: your face or a simple mark, readable at the size of a fingernail. Banner: your name, what you stream, when you stream. No phone numbers, no home address, no school name.
Bio: one sentence of what the channel is, one of when you are live, one link. Under 150 characters so it shows without a tap.
Settings that matter on day one: date of birth truthfully, two-factor authentication on, email verified, a recovery phone. Country is whatever is true for you.
Twitch needs a stream key to go live from a computer. That key is a password. You will never read it aloud, never type it in a chat, never show it on screen.
steps: Check the handle on four platforms.
Create or rename the channel on Twitch and one other platform.
Upload a profile picture and a banner.
Write the bio.
Turn on two-factor and verify the email.
assignment: Two channels set up with picture, banner, bio and two-factor on. Post the two links in the cohort group.

title: Audio first
summary: Viewers forgive a blurry picture and never forgive bad sound. This class is about hearing yourself the way they hear you.
body: The microphone should be close to your mouth, 10 to 20 cm. Distance is the enemy; every doubling of distance halves the voice and doubles the room.

Cheapest big upgrade: a wired lavalier mic that clips to your shirt, US$15 to 25, plugs into the phone or the laptop. Second cheapest: any gaming headset. A ring light with a built-in mic is not a microphone.
Room: soft things absorb echo. Curtains, a bed, a wardrobe behind you. A bare tiled room sounds like a bathroom.
Levels: your voice should peak at about three quarters of the meter and never hit the red. Game or music under your voice, never over it. Set it once and leave it.
Monitor yourself: record 30 seconds, play it back with headphones, listen for hiss, hum, fan, echo, and the fridge. Fix one thing at a time.
steps: Record 30 seconds on the phone and listen with headphones.
Move the mic closer, record again, compare.
Kill the loudest background noise you can find.
Set the voice level to three quarters of the meter.
Record a final 30 seconds and keep it.
assignment: A five-minute live where at least one viewer says in chat that the audio is clean. Screenshot that message.
checklist: No fan or fridge in the recording

title: The computer stream
summary: OBS Studio from zero. Scenes, sources, the stream key, the settings that stop dropped frames.
body: OBS Studio is free and runs on any laptop. Streamlabs is OBS with training wheels; use it if OBS feels like too much. Both do the same job.
A scene is a screen layout. A source is one thing in it: your camera, your game, a picture, text. You build scenes once and switch between them live.

Settings for a Berbice connection: Output mode Simple, encoder NVIDIA NVENC if the laptop has a GeForce, otherwise x264 at preset veryfast. Bitrate 2500 kbps on wifi, 4500 on a wire, 6000 only if the speed test shows 10 Mbps upload or more. Resolution 1280x720 at 30 fps to start. Move up only when dropped frames stay at zero.
The stream key goes in Settings, Stream, pasted from the Twitch dashboard. If anyone sees it, reset it on the dashboard immediately.
Stats window (View, Stats): dropped frames must stay at zero. If they climb, lower the bitrate by 500 and try again. Wired internet beats wifi every single time.
steps: Install OBS Studio from obsproject.com.
Add a scene called Live with your camera and a text source with your name.
Paste the stream key from the Twitch dashboard. Never type it anywhere else.
Set 720p30 and 2500 kbps.
Stream two minutes with the title test, watch Stats, stop.
assignment: First OBS stream with the Stats window open. Screenshot Stats showing zero dropped frames.

title: Scenes and brand
summary: Five scenes every channel needs, built from the Little Rock Twitch kit as the template so yours looks finished on day one.
body: The five scenes: Starting Soon, Live, Just Chatting, BRB, Ending. Each one has a card image, your name somewhere, and sound. Starting Soon with music tells people the stream is real and about to begin.
The name bug: your handle in a corner, small, always on. A chat overlay so viewers see their own words on screen. Alerts for new followers if the platform offers them.
Colour: pick two. One dark, one bright. Use them everywhere: cards, text, banner. Rockland Streamer University's own are storm navy and lightning blue; yours are yours.
Images are 1920x1080 for cards and overlays, 800x800 for the profile picture, 1200x480 for the banner. Keep the important part of every image in the middle; phones crop the edges.
Music under Starting Soon and BRB: the 88.5 Rock FM stream is cleared for every student in this school. Any other music must be yours or from the platform's own library.
steps: Make five cards in Canva or any editor at 1920x1080 with your two colours.
Build the five scenes in OBS with the cards as image sources.
Add the name bug and the chat overlay to Live.
Add the 88.5 stream URL as a media source on Starting Soon and BRB.
Set hotkeys to switch scenes.
assignment: Five-scene collection built. Screenshot the OBS scene list and one card.

title: Talk to nobody, then to everybody
summary: Hosting an empty room without dying inside, reading chat, the hook, and the schedule that makes people come back.
body: Every streamer started with zero viewers. Talk anyway. The recording becomes clips; the habit becomes the show. Pretend one friend is watching and talk to them.
The hook is the first 30 seconds: what is happening today, why it matters, what you are about to do. Say it again every ten minutes for the people who just arrived.
Reading chat: say the person's name, read the message, answer it. Nothing grows a channel faster than being seen. Never read out anything private someone types; say it was received.
Silence is fine for ten seconds. Longer than that, narrate what you are doing. Describe, react, ask the room a question.
A schedule beats talent. Same day, same time, every week, and say it at the end of every stream. Put it in the bio. People plan around it.
steps: Write your 30-second hook on paper. Say it three times.
Pick a weekly day and time and put it in your bio.
Go live at that exact time with the Starting Soon scene for three minutes first.
Stream 30 minutes. Read every message by name.
End with the schedule line.
assignment: A 30-minute stream at a pre-announced time. Post the announcement and the VOD link.

title: Games on stream
summary: Capturing a PC game, a console, or a browser game, with your face on it and your frame rate intact.
body: Game Capture source in OBS for PC games, set to capture any fullscreen application. Window Capture for browser games such as the PINKLAND games at pinkland.gy, which are free to stream and made in Berbice.
Consoles need a capture card (US$60 and up) between the console and the TV. Or stream straight from the console's own Twitch app and skip OBS until you can afford the card.
Frame rate: the game and the stream share the graphics card. On a laptop, cap the game at 60 fps, set the stream at 720p30 or 1080p30, and use NVENC so the stream encodes on the card's own chip.
Fortnite settings for streaming: Fullscreen, frame limit at the screen refresh rate, DLSS Quality, Nanite and Lumen off, hardware ray tracing off. Looks fine, runs steady.

Content rule for this school: family-friendly. Pink paint, never gore. No voice chat from strangers on stream; disable party chat capture or mute it. You are responsible for every word on your channel.
steps: Add a Game Capture or Window Capture source to Live.
Add the webcam as a small circle in a corner.
Cap the game frame rate and turn ray tracing off.
Stream 20 minutes of a game; watch Stats for dropped frames.
Clip one good moment.
assignment: A game stream with a webcam in the corner. Post the VOD and a 30-second clip.

kind: Self-paced, with a live Q&A with Naomi
title: Music and the law
summary: What gets a channel muted, struck or banned, and how to never worry about it. Taught by Naomi, a lawyer.
body: Copyright: the person who made a song owns it. Playing it on your stream is a public performance and the platform's robots know every song. Twitch mutes VODs, YouTube strikes the channel, three strikes and the channel is gone.
Fair use is not a magic word. Reacting to a song, playing it quietly, playing only 30 seconds: none of these protect you. Only cleared music protects you.

Cleared for this school: the 88.5 Rock FM live stream as background on your Starting Soon and BRB scenes. Twitch Soundtrack, YouTube Audio Library and the platform's own music tools are cleared for everyone.
Games are usually fine to stream; publishers want it. Films, TV, sports and other people's streams are not. Reading the news is fine; reading a whole article aloud is not.

Other people's faces and voices: in public, generally fine; in private spaces, ask. Children are a separate rule set, covered in lesson 10. When a copyright claim arrives, do not panic and do not ignore it: remove the content, read the notice, ask in the cohort group.
steps: Replace every piece of uncleared music in your scenes.
Turn off game music if the game uses licensed songs (Fortnite radio, sports games).
Read your platform's copyright page once, slowly.
Write down what you will do if a claim arrives.
Bring one question to the Saturday Q&A.
assignment: A stream using only cleared audio, with a one-line note in the group of what you changed.

title: Money
summary: How a streamer in Guyana actually gets paid, platform by platform, and the one-page revenue plan every graduate leaves with.
body: Twitch Affiliate: 50 followers, 7 stream days in 30, 3 average viewers. Unlocks subscriptions and Bits. Payout by PayPal or bank transfer, minimum US$50. Partner comes later and is not needed to earn.
YouTube Partner: 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours, or 10 million Shorts views. Ads, memberships, Super Chat. Payout needs a verified AdSense account.
TikTok LIVE gifts: viewers send gifts, you cash out diamonds. Available in some countries only; check your account's eligibility before planning around it.

Sponsors and selling: the money that does not depend on a platform. A local business pays for a mention; a seller streams the stall and takes orders in chat; a link in bio goes to a Shopify page. Little Rock's advertiser list is a template for how to price a mention.
Taxes and records: income is income. Keep a simple sheet of every payout. Platforms ask for tax forms; fill them truthfully. Never let anyone else's account receive your money.
steps: Check which monetisation your platforms allow for your account today.
Write what a mention on your stream would cost, in GY$.
List three local businesses who could sponsor you.
Set up the payout method on one platform.
Fill the one-page revenue plan template from the group.
assignment: A one-page revenue plan: platform money, sponsor money, selling money, and the first target date for each.

title: Safety and minors
summary: Doxxing, location leaks, kids on camera, moderation settings, and the moment you stop a stream.
body: Never on stream: your address, your school, your workplace schedule, a view out the window that places your house, documents on the desk, a package label, a car number plate.

Kids: platforms require 13 and up, with guardian involvement under 18. In this school, students under 18 stream with a guardian who has signed and who is present for the first live. Other children, yours or anyone's, stay off camera unless their guardian has agreed in writing.

Moderation: AutoMod on, level 2 or higher. Followers-only chat if trolls arrive. Name one moderator before your first public stream and give them the power to time out and ban. Block and move on; never argue.
Private messages: anyone offering money, sponsorships or gifts by DM wants something. Verified brand emails only, and ask the cohort group before answering.

Stop the stream when: someone in chat posts your private information, a child walks on camera, you feel unsafe, or you are too tired to think. Ending early costs nothing. Say you will be back and end it.
steps: Walk through your streaming room on camera and remove everything that places or names you.
Turn on AutoMod and set the level.
Appoint a moderator and tell them the rules.
Set DMs to friends only on every platform.
Write the three things that would make you end a stream.
assignment: Screenshot of your moderation settings and the name of your moderator posted in the group.

title: Clips, VODs and growth
summary: One stream becomes ten posts. Clipping, shorts, titles, thumbnails and a posting rhythm that fits around a job.
body: A stream is raw material. The VOD is the record; the clips are the advertising. Three clips per stream, 15 to 60 seconds, posted as TikToks, Reels and Shorts the next day.
A clip needs a first second that explains itself. Trim until the moment starts immediately. Add captions; most phones watch muted.
Titles say what happens, not what you are: 'Lost the final with one HP' beats 'Stream highlights'. Thumbnails: a face, big text, three words, your two colours.
Rhythm: stream twice a week, post three clips a day after each stream, one post on the off days. That is ten posts from two streams. Batch the editing into one hour.
Measure one number: average viewers on Twitch, watch time on YouTube, views on TikTok. Look at it weekly, not hourly. Growth is boring and slow and then sudden.
steps: Watch your last VOD and mark three moments.
Clip them to under 60 seconds each with captions.
Write a title that says what happens.
Post one to TikTok, one to Shorts, one to Reels.
Write your weekly rhythm in the bio.
assignment: Three clips from your own VOD posted on three platforms. Links in the group.

title: The graduation stream
summary: A one-hour show on the Rockland Streamer University stage, on your own channel and the Streamer U team, judged live.
body: Your graduation project is a one-hour stream in your track: a game session, a talk show, a live sale, a reporting hit, or an event. Announced a week before. On schedule.

The stage: your channel is added to the Rockland Streamer University Twitch team for the day, Channel 10 live carries highlights, and 88.5 reads the lineup on air. Family in Berbice and the diaspora can watch from lrtvs.gy.
Judging, live, by Naomi and two graduates or guests: audio, hook, chat handling, brand, safety, and whether the hour had a shape (a start, a middle, an end).
You graduate with a numbered certificate, a place on the team, a listing on the graduates wall, and first call for guest slots on 88.5 and Channel 10.
Then you keep the schedule you set in lesson 6. The school was six weeks. The channel is yours for as long as you show up.
steps: Pick the graduation show in your track and announce it a week ahead.
Rehearse the hook and the ending.
Check audio, scenes, moderation and the room the day before.
Go live at your slot. One hour. Read chat by name.
Say your schedule, thank the room, end on time.
